title: A string of beads
hookLine: some keep count of simran on a string of beads

lines: A LOOP OF BEADS IN THE FINGERS.
cards: Watch the hands of an older Sikh man at the back of a gurdwara, or a grandmother on a bus in Punjab. Sometimes a small loop of beads moves through the fingers, one at a time, while the lips move very slightly.
No book open. No phone. Just thumb, bead, thumb, bead.
Your grandparents may have done this too, in whatever tradition they came from: people all over the world have found that hands like having something to hold while the heart remembers.

teach.b: It's called a mala, which simply means a garland or a string. A Sikh mala is often made of wool, or of iron or steel beads, and many have one hundred and eight, though smaller ones are common too.
Some Nihang Sikhs, the traditional warrior order in blue, wear large malas around the neck or wrist. The use is simple.
With each bead, you say the Name once, usually Waheguru, and move on. The mala keeps count so the mind doesn't have to, and it gives restless fingers something to do. Here's the interesting part.

The Guru Granth Sahib is honest that beads on their own do nothing. The Gurus and the saints in the Granth were sharp about outward show: counting beads for others to see while the heart is elsewhere.
Kabir, one of the saints whose verses are in the Granth, turns the whole idea around.
In paraphrase: my mala is my tongue, and the Name of the Lord is strung on it. The real string of beads is inside. So Sikhs hold the mala lightly.
Many use one gladly as a help. Many never use one at all, and the Sikh code of conduct doesn't require it. Both are at home in the gurdwara.
The point is never the count.
Each bead is one more moment of remembering, and a hundred and eight small moments add up to something.

how: Some Sikhs use a mala, often of wool or iron beads, to count repetitions of Waheguru during simran; many others do simran without one, and the Sikh code of conduct does not require it.

o: a small book of the morning hymns
a string of beads for counting the Name
a holy cord tied on the wrist for luck

games.q: what's inside the word — tap the pairs.
p: a garland, a string of beads
the beads on a full mala
a quarter of a full mala

s: every Sikh is required to use a mala
some use one gladly; many never do, and the Sikh code of conduct doesn't require it.
a saint in the Guru Granth Sahib says the real mala is the tongue
Kabir: my mala is my tongue, and the Name is strung on it.
the Granth teaches that counting beads earns merit by itself
it warns that beads alone, without the heart, do nothing.

games.q: you've got a mala, and you realize you've counted twenty beads while planning your week. what does the Granth's view suggest?
o: the count still counts: the beads did the work.
throw the mala away: it's only for show.
come back and let the next bead be real remembering.
games.why: beads alone do nothing, but they aren't forbidden either. the point is the remembering, one bead at a time.

practice: No beads needed: touch your thumb to each finger segment in turn, three segments on four fingers for twelve, then around again and a bit more, for twenty-seven, a quarter of a full mala.
With each touch, say one word silently, Waheguru if you pray, or simply feel your breath if you'd rather. Lose count? Start again wherever you are.

wordCard.voice: Mala. A garland, a string of beads, often a hundred and eight, that some Sikhs use to count the Name.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: a garland, a string of beads for counting the Name.

carryVoice: Your line: bead by bead. The real string is the one inside. Day one hundred twenty-five, done.
